reading_text: The birch put out its leaves before any other tree, though the ground beneath the house was still cold and the mornings still bit at the windows. That first green is the home you were raised in, opening before it was safe to, feeding what came after. Now the meltwater runs down under those roots, quiet and unseen, carrying warmth to the wood before you notice any change above. The way you read a room, the mood at the table before a word is spoken, moves the same way. Keep tending it as you are, and the tree grows into one that others gather under, some staying near the trunk and some setting off with a cutting of it in hand. When the choice ahead sits in front of you, will it be the door of the old house you are weighing, or a room in it you have not yet walked into?

The slope was here long before the water, its hollows and stone laid down and not yet named. Now the water moves over it, feeling out the low places, turning where the ground turns, and no hand shows it the way. This is the work finding its own line before you have decided on one, Anna, the slow test of every dip and edge. Keep on as you are and the small turnings gather into a channel, one that holds the water and carries it further down. The way down is being cut by the going, and you are the water on the slope.

The keys to the old house still lie in your palm, Anna, worn smooth where two hands once passed things back and forth across the same table. That balance between giving and taking held the walls up longer than the timber did. Something of that exchange stayed in you when the door closed, quiet in the dark like a seed that has not yet decided to open. It grows on its own time, and no amount of watching it hurries the ground. Yet your hand keeps closing around keys to a house you no longer live in, and that grip is the hard part, Anna, holding what was yours while the roof belongs to someone else now. The keys are still warm from your palm, and the house stands where you left it.

The valley behind you held the road steady, sheltered between two ridges where the wind never reached the path itself. Now the road passes the old farmstead, the turf roof settling back into the ground it came from, and you feel the pull of the walls that raised you even as your feet keep going. The friction is here — you cannot carry the whole house forward, and some of what shaped you belongs to the ground you are walking off. Ahead the road winds along the river and disappears around the next bend, keeping the water's pace, neither hurried nor held back. This is the road doing what a road does — it goes, and it does not show you what waits past the turn. The river runs on beside you, and the walking is enough.

Long before you came to this fork, a seed was set in the dark ground of you, and it has been quietly gathering its own strength there, unhurried. That much is settled; it does not need your permission to have grown. Now the grey lifts off the scree at first light, and the loose stone that has held its slope through every spring storm shows plain against the brightening sky. You are standing where the path splits below that slope, and the light is reaching both ways at once. Keep walking as you walk now, and the same raw force that packed that scree tight enough to withstand the storms is the force that carries you down whichever track you choose. The stone does not shift, and it does not decide; it only holds.

A voice reached you once across the water, Anna, and its words are woven now into what was — they cannot be unsaid, and they carried you to this bank. The line runs down from your hand into the dark water, and nothing has touched it yet. What lies below is not decided, only waiting, and the surface holds still while you hold still. The far edge of that water is a narrow gap in the rocks, and if you keep drifting as you are the current will take you toward it. It is a threshold, and it asks to be met slowly, not rushed. When the line finally pulls, will you know whether you want what has taken it?

The iron lay cold in the dark shed through a long waiting, holding its shape and giving nothing, and that stillness is set now, it cannot be unmade. But the forge is lit, and the coals breathe heat into the metal until it softens and begins to move under the hammer. This is the warmth passed into a thing until it is willing to change form. Keep feeding that fire and the iron takes an edge, glowing where the dark shed was blind before. The light in the forge shows the hand its own work. What the fire wakes does not go back to sleep.

The horse carried you across the grey glacial river before you could see the ford, its footing sure where the water ran fast and cold over black sand. You trusted the crossing to something steadier than your own eyes, and that crossing is behind you now, already made. On the far bank the horse grazes, warm-flanked and easy, its strength no longer spent on the water but returning to it slowly, the way a body fills again once the hard reach is done. What you carried across is still yours, lighter now for having moved. The path from here leads up toward low turf roofs and a doorway that has stood a long time, the kind of place where a rider unsaddles and lets the horse rest in the paddock it knows. Keep walking as you are, and the ground softens toward home, toward the fire and the long quiet after.
